# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

docs/competition/competition-deals.md:10:# Competition deals
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:12:This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:14:The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:16:## Deal identity within an event
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:18:A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:20:For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:22:The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:24:## The format already implemented
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:26:`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:28:`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:30:The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:32:The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:34:## Why a code repeats an arrangement
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:36:The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:44:## Freshness is narrower in the current session
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:46:The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:48:`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:50:That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:54:## Starting state and saved progress
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:56:`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:58:`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md) explain those existing fields.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:60:The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:62:## What reproducibility can establish
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:66:During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:68:[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:3:  description: Entry-order seeds and opening pairings for four- and eight-person
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:9:# Competition pairing
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:11:This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:13:Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:15:## From the entry list to the opening matches
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:17:Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:36:## What a seed means here
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:38:In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:40:This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:42:There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:44:[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:46:## The small example catches a different mistake
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:54:## A pairing review on paper
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:56:A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:58:This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:60:The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:64:## Unresolved pairing decisions
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:10:# Boards used in competition
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:12:This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:14:A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in [competition deals](competition-deals.md).
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:16:## Dimensions by stage
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:18:Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:26:The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:28:The stage vocabulary itself belongs to [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md). The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:30:## Existing support in the core
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:34:`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:36:`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:40:## What the larger face set actually changes
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:42:The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:44:All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:46:For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:50:## Board dimensions in the layout
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:52:`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:54:In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:56:The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:58:This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [layout grid](../visuals/layout-grid.md) and [zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md).
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:60:## Positions remain positions
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:62:The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:64:This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:66:Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md) covers the existing behavior.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:68:## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:70:The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:72:How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:74:One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:4:    honest boundary around the solo implementation.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:10:# Shared-device competition
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:14:Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:16:## Where the product stands
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:18:The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:20:This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:24:## Why share a device
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:32:## Three things people are following
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:34:An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:36:These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:38:The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:40:## A local social activity, with local evidence
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:42:The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:48:## How the current code helps
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:50:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:54:The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:3:  description: Playtests about face recognition, keyboard travel, device handoff
docs/competition/competition-research.md:10:# Shared-device playtest notes
docs/competition/competition-research.md:16:## Session setting
docs/competition/competition-research.md:22:The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:24:## Laptop: learning the faces aloud
docs/competition/competition-research.md:26:In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”
docs/competition/competition-research.md:28:Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:30:This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:34:## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation
docs/competition/competition-research.md:36:Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:40:Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:42:The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:44:## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own
docs/competition/competition-research.md:48:The next player first adjusted the tablet on the table, then looked for the board. That sequence would have been easy to describe as slow play if the observer had measured from physical handoff. It was mostly positioning the device. The observation helped separate the social transition from actual interaction with the game.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:50:People also used the visible completed board as a conversation piece. They pointed at remembered mistakes and explained how they finally located a pair. The exposed cards carried a short history of the attempt that a bare result number would not capture. In a group setting, that retrospective conversation was part of the appeal.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:54:## Phone: scrolling and tapping had different purposes
docs/competition/competition-research.md:56:On the phone, Niko sometimes touched the board to move its visible area rather than to reveal a card. His comments made that intention clear: he was searching for a remembered row near the edge. A raw touch trace would have contained contact with several cards, but contact alone would not have described the intended action.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:60:The observer's view was narrower on the phone too. People beside the player often saw the device's back or an oblique angle, so they talked more about the eventual result than about individual reveals. That was a different social experience from the laptop, even though the underlying card actions were unchanged. [Pointer and touch](../interface/pointer-and-touch.md) and [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md) cover the relevant existing behavior.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:62:## The mismatch pause helped memory and confused tapping
docs/competition/competition-research.md:68:## Spectators remembered more than the current player expected
docs/competition/competition-research.md:70:People who watched closely often remembered a location that the player had forgotten. Sometimes that produced a laugh; sometimes it produced an unsolicited hint. When the device moved out of view, conversation changed from specific positions to general encouragement. The physical setting strongly influenced how much information was shared.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:72:This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:76:## Evidence retained from the discussion
docs/competition/competition-research.md:78:These sessions identified misunderstandings during local play. Shape-only memory, keyboard travel, device adjustment and the visible mismatch interval each explain a different kind of report. The observations are useful starting points for further sessions.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:80:A board code can anchor an arrangement, a snapshot can anchor progress and a replay can anchor actions. The observer's account adds the human context those artifacts omit. [Competition deals](competition-deals.md), [browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) and [acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) explain the technical evidence.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:10:# Competition rounds
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:12:This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:14:A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:16:## Names during play
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:18:The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:22:The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:24:## Round, match and board are different contexts
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:26:A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:28:Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:30:This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:32:## What the current status component knows
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:34:`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:36:The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:38:Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. [Status bar](../interface/status-bar.md) explains the existing statistics, and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains the surrounding composition.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:40:This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:42:## A generation is not a round counter
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:44:The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:46:That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:48:The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:52:## How a sequence can be reviewed
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:54:A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:56:The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:10:# Competition results and local records
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:14:The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:16:## The competition boundary
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:18:A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:20:For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:24:## What the game saves today
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:26:`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:41:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:45:[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:47:## Two ordinary paths have side effects
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:49:The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:57:## Where saving actually happens
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:63:The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:67:## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:71:That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:75:## A concrete review example
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:77:Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:79:The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:3:  description: Ordered result comparison, active-time precision, and seed priority
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:10:# Comparing tied competition results
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:12:This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:14:A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:16:## Comparison order
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:18:Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:34:## When every recorded value looks equal
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:36:Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:38:A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:40:The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:42:## Active time in the current game
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:52:## Display precision is a separate concern
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:54:`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:56:The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:58:Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:62:## Pauses and interruptions
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:64:The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:72:## Completion and boundary values
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:74:`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:80:## Useful evidence for a disagreement
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:84:A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:86:For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) for the exact validation and React effect. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md).

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. [Offline delivery](../architecture/offline-delivery.md) describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, [Retention policy](retention-policy.md) concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

[Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.
